activity.text: More businesses are building teams beyond their payroll, working with freelancers, contractors, agencies and fractional specialists. This gives them access to specialised talent, the flexibility to scale and the ability to move faster without hiring every capability full-time. But the way we manage external work hasn’t kept pace. Businesses are often left choosing between micromanaging people and having little visibility into the work. We’re building Fortal to give business a control, visibility and a secure way to collaborate with external teams. Fortal transforms your browser into a private workspace where you can give external teams secure access, collaborate live and see work getting done live. Business just had its Ozempic moment with AI 💉 Hear me out! The weight and bloat came off fast, mostly in the form of talent. Then came the side effects: sluggish growth, missing junior talent, eye-watering token bills and humans being rehired to supervise the robots that replaced them. For genuinely bloated companies, the jab helped. For everyone else, the 'miracle AI injection' is starting to look rather expensive. The winners won't be the companies that lose the most weight. They'll be the ones that work out the right dose before they lose muscle along with the fat. I wouldn't be surprised if, over the next few years, companies scrutinize software spend with the same intensity they once reserved for office space and travel budgets. Most SaaS companies are doing exactly what they should. They're monetising usage. The more tools become embedded in day-to-day work, the bigger a line item software becomes. The recent conversation around AI token costs is making conversation around software costs more visible. But founders of small and medium-sized businesses, many of which now rely on 20–25 SaaS applications, have been feeling the pinch for a while. Every new employee, freelancer or agency often means another ChatGPT seat. Another Figma licence. Another CRM user. Another project management account. Unlike payroll, software spend doesn't necessarily compound in value. A great hire can create many times more value than they cost but a tool most likely doesn't. It's one of the reasons we've been thinking so much about access at Fortal Businesses increasingly rely on external specialists, agencies and freelancers, but today's default answer is still to buy more software licenses or share existing ones. Neither feels like the right long-term solution. If software is becoming one of the biggest costs of growth, then giving people secure access to the tools they need, without multiplying licenses every time your team changes, starts to feel like a much more important problem to solve. One of the things that has surprised me most while building Fortal is how much of modern business still leans on flimsy guardrails to protect proprietary data and assets. Businesses are working with more freelancers, agencies, virtual assistants and external teams than ever before. Yet the process often looks like this: ✔️ Sign an NDA. ✔️ Share passwords. ✔️ Hope nothing goes wrong. NDAs absolutely have their place, but they don't prevent a breach. They define what happens after one. I believe the future of external collaboration is about making trust & control compatible. That's one of the core ideas behind Fortal and why we believe technology should play a much bigger role in protecting businesses than paperwork alone. I also think this represents an opportunity for freelancers. As businesses become more security conscious, the freelancers who can offer a more secure and privacy-first way of working will naturally stand out. Trust is becoming part of the value proposition, not just the work itself. The freelancers who help clients protect their data won't just differentiate themselves, they'll be better positioned to win larger, longer-term and more sensitive projects. One of the biggest bottlenecks in work today isn't execution itself. 𝐈𝐭'𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. Business owners wait for updates. Project managers spend hours chasing them. Teams interrupt their work to write them. That's a huge amount of capacity spent explaining work instead of doing it. Meanwhile, most execution remains hidden between status updates, stand-ups, and meetings. By the time a project turns red, the warning signs were usually there all along, they just weren't visible. Meta just appointed Kunal Shah, the founder of CRED, to lead WhatsApp and its 3 billion users. The immediate reaction online: Meta is quietly buying a path into Indians' financial data. I read it differently. This looks less like a data grab and more like a numbers game. India is WhatsApp's single largest market with est. 850M users. If you want to turn a messaging app into a commerce and payments engine, you don't start where the platform is small. You start where it's already in everyone's pocket. And you put someone in charge who understands that market natively. Shah didn't build a messaging product. He built trust around money in India, at scale. That's the real signal. WhatsApp's next chapter isn't about messages. It's about transactions. The part to watch out isn't that Meta wants your financial data. It's that Meta already has the distribution to make payments feel inevitable. Not a new app to download. A behaviour you already have. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗯𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲. For the past six weeks, I've been part of a cohort of early-stage founders led by Vidya Narayanan an exceptional entrepreneur who has built multiple companies and brings hard won experience from every stage of the startup journey. Vidya generously, candidly, and often bluntly shared lessons on what works, when to pivot, what to ignore, and how entrepreneurship itself is changing at a time when the pace of change feels faster than ever. Just as valuable was the cohort itself. I had the opportunity to learn alongside an incredible group of founders who are building meaningful products and tackling some of today's most important challenges. The quality of thinking, openness, and willingness to share lessons made every session worthwhile. Zachary Lynde Maddy A. Mohsin A. Anuram Vajrapu Cesare Mercurio Sushmitha Kanukurthi The conversations about challenges being faced right now, decisions being made in real time, and lessons being learned through experience rather than hindsight is what I am walking away with above everything else. Special thanks also to Sana Afreen for bringing the cohort together. If you're an early-stage founder, I'd highly recommend joining one of the upcoming cohorts. The sessions are valuable, but the value compounds with the people in the room and the opportunity to learn from founders who are actively building, experimenting, and navigating the same challenges you are. I'd also encourage you to follow the journeys of the founders in the cohort. Some are building remarkable companies, and I suspect we'll be hearing a lot more about many of them in the years ahead. ...more

Building your life and work on your own terms makes you unemployable. Because once you've architected your life in a certain way, the idea of asking permission to live the old way seems insane. I'm not sure if that's a good or bad thing. But I'm certain it's a true thing. The challenge is that getting this whole equation right is both difficult and daunting. If you haven't started, the biggest question is...how do I start? If you've already started, the biggest question is...how do I survive? And those are two of the most difficult questions to answer because there's no such thing as a right one. Rather than try, I did what I thought was the best thing: I put together a free 30-page field manual on the 7 learned behaviors of successful entrepreneurs. From 10 hours of interviews and voice notes, 250+ essays, and hundreds of conversations with entrepreneurs over the years. Read it free here: https://buff.ly/qyPzps4 I hope you enjoy it and it helps you create your own answer to those questions. Feel free to leave any feedback below. ...more ...more

Perks of being a Vibe Marketing Tech Fest (VMF) Board Advisor: VIP seat next to Kevin Chesters . I ended up being his entertainer, just as I did in my first job, when I was paid to talk to people (and occasionally drink). Charged by the hour back then. Now maybe accumulated wisdom finally qualifies me for a subscription. :) Somewhere between talking and laughing, Kevin and I interrogated the advertising industry, creativity and this funny thing we humans have done with it. Creativity is probably one of the most inborn human traits, and creative problem solving is why we are still here. Also possibly the reason why AI might be the end of us. :) Yet with time we somehow learned to delegate creativity to creative departments, while the rest of us got busy with more serious things apparently. Kevin's mum brought him up to question and challenge everything. He obviously took it seriously, still challenging superficial truths and established rules of the game. Maybe my love of Dubito ergo cogito, cogito ergo sum is what brought us together. ( I doubt, therefore I think. I think, therefore I am.) After all, it earned me a personalised signature in The Creative Nudge, a book full of small quirks to wake us up and start thinking again. Equally pretty in design. And look at that perfect shade of yellow. Adorable. :) Through my life I've been called various pet names by some very dear people , often learning a new English word in the process. Lass. Muse. Bizcochito. Now Kevin has added “hoot”, I’ll happily take it. And thanx to Vibe Marketing Tech Fest (VMF) and Markee Awards for lovely hospitality and even lovelier content! Harsha Thawani was my partner in crime that night. Alas, our beautiful photo somehow got lost, so I guess we will just have to repeat the night out. Was great seeing and reconnecting with so many familiar faces. Till the next time!

Most people I know don't love their job. They get on with it & just make it work. But me, I loved mine. All 12 years of it. Truly the best job I could have ever asked for and that is probably why it’s taken me almost a month to share this. But, I owe it to Lifebuoy, and to the people who gave me wings to live the most incredible years of my life to pen this down. So here goes.. a love letter perhaps? I joined Lifebuoy for one reason: it’s purpose to help people live better and healthier lives. As luck would have it, I landed a global role that came with the privilege of experiencing this show up every single place I went. The chars of Bangladesh, where there wasn't a single medical centre but there was Lifebuoy, caring for people. In Nepal, weeks after the 2015 earthquake as I sat with families, next to me a stack of soaps because after the disaster comes the disease, rampant, deadly. In Africa where +300m children suffer from Trachoma, a type of blindness preventable through regular handwashing. Forty-two countries. The world's largest behavior change programme. All of it built around something as ordinary and mundane as washing your hands with soap. Simple right? It never was. The challenge was never the soap. It was people. How do you make something ordinary feel important? How do you make something people know they should do, become something they want to do. That's where the magic happened, that beautiful overlap between behavior science and marketing. Only possible because of the coming together of such amazing professionals from public health, advertising, R&D, marketing, finance and more. Working with such world class experts to bring change communities across the world gave me meaning, it was truly a gift. There were of course many who challenged us, we were not bringing immediate profits. But what we did bring was a deep love for our brand. This work brought belief, hope, trust for millions around the world. I saw it, I heard it, and more importantly I felt it. Every single time I was on the ground, I was reminded that what we do matters. I leave Unilever with an even stronger belief that businesses & brands can be a tremendous force for good. We're so incredibly privileged to touch billions of lives through the products we make, my hope is we never stop asking ourselves how we can use that privilege for the benefit of people, communities and the planet at large. I have so many people to thank, Lifebuoy will always have the biggest piece of my heart now of course shared with my 3 year old and a new adventure! From today, I launch my independent consulting practice. Excited to continue to work at the intersection of health, sustainability and social impact, helping people and organizations do and live better. If this speaks to you I’d would love to connect and chat. For now, time to sign off from this incredible chapter in true Lifebuoy style ‘Once a Lifesaver always a Lifesaver’

A founder gave me forty minutes on his technology last month. Sensors, accuracy rates, the physics of the thing. All of it genuinely impressive. Then, I asked what changes for the customer. And he only needed 11 words for it. This is most of what I actually do. Not invent a message. Remove the forty minutes people put in front of the one true sentence. Usually, because the forty minutes is what they think, is important. The uncomfortable part is that this works the same way on a life. Ask someone what they are building and you get the pitch. Ask what changes if it works and something much smaller and much more fun arrives.

Of software Engineers 19 months ago, I fell out of CPG and data analytics and into technology, software and cloud infrastructure. It has been a fascinating shift and a serious learning curve. I have a new level of respect for engineers and software developers and the tech ecosystem. But I keep coming back to one thought. The real unlock will happen when engineers start building more deliberately for non-engineers, and when more people cross disciplines to help shape what gets built. Technology needs more translators between worlds. People who understand the problem, the user and the technology well enough to connect all three. #meltingpot

Get out. Get out of that sh*tty job, relationship, marriage, friendship, whatever it is that has turned your days into something you merely survive. Yes, it will hurt like a b*tch for a while. You will question the decision, miss the familiar, replay old conversations, and occasionally romanticize the very thing that was breaking you. Human beings are strange like that. We can miss a prison simply because we knew where the walls were. But sooner or later, the fog will lift and you will feel better. You will begin sleeping better. Your body will relax. Your mind will stop preparing for the next argument, the next insult, the next Monday morning, whatever next performance is. And one day you catch yourself laughing freely and realize how long it had been since life felt light. You know the hardest part of leaving is not the leaving. It is 'accepting' that something you invested years in cannot be repaired by investing more years. That is because confuse endurance with virtue because society rewards people who “adjust.” Families say, “Thoda compromise karo.” Offices say, “Every workplace has problems.” Friends say, “Give it another chance.” But how many chances does something get before it starts eating your life? Yes, there is courage in staying when something deserves saving. But there is equal courage in walking away when staying has become self-harm. I am just saying you have one life. Do not spend it proving how much pain you can tolerate. Get out and live it well.
